name: Grape seed extract
short: Case report: recurrent vomiting, diarrhoea and weakness, resolving on stopping. Phlebotonics as a group: slightly more adverse events than placebo. Lab: CYP3A4 and platelet inhibition.
text: A case report describes a 49-year-old man with recurrent nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and acute weakness after taking a grape seed extract supplement, with no other cause found; symptoms resolved when he stopped and he remained symptom-free 5 years later, and the authors note the lack of controlled trials detailing its adverse-effect profile. A 2020 Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials of oral phlebotonics for chronic venous insufficiency (rutosides, hidrosmine and diosmine, calcium dobesilate, Centella asiatica, aminaftone, French maritime pine bark extract and grape seed extract; one of the 56 trials with usable efficacy data was on grape seed extract) found that phlebotonics as a group probably increase adverse events slightly compared with placebo (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.27; 37 studies; 5789 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), most often gastrointestinal disorders, with no separate figures for grape seed extract. On interactions, the evidence is mixed and mostly laboratory-based: a review of P450-mediated herb-drug interactions judged adverse interactions unlikely when grape seed extract is taken with prescription drugs that are CYP substrates, whereas a laboratory study in human liver microsomes found grape seed to be a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4 metabolism of midazolam and docetaxel and called for clinical studies. Laboratory studies also found that grape seed extract reduced platelet aggregation in vitro, and one reported a distinct effect on plasma coagulation tests only at the higher concentration tested; the abstracts do not report bleeding in people or test anticoagulant medicines.
